sections.title: Introduction
rules: Clustering is an unsupervised learning task that groups unlabeled data into clusters of similar instances.
Clustering discovers natural groupings and structures within unannotated datasets.
Vector quantization uses cluster prototypes to compress large datasets and images.
Common applications include customer segmentation, image compression, document organization, and biological sequence grouping.

sections.title: Mixture Densities
rules: A mixture density models a probability distribution as a weighted sum of k component densities.
Each mixture component represents a distinct group or cluster.
Mixture proportions represent prior probabilities of individual components and must sum to one.
Gaussian mixture models represent each component density with a multivariate normal distribution.
The parameters of a Gaussian mixture include component priors, mean vectors, and covariance matrices.

sections.title: k-Means Clustering
rules: The k-means algorithm partitions data into k non-overlapping clusters.
The objective function minimizes the sum of squared Euclidean distances between points and their assigned cluster centers.
The algorithm initializes k cluster centers randomly or from selected data points.
In the assignment step, the algorithm assigns each data point to its nearest cluster center.
In the update step, the algorithm recomputes each cluster center as the mean of its assigned points.
The algorithm alternates between assignment and update steps until cluster centers stop changing.
The k-means algorithm converges to a local minimum of the objective function.
Initialization influences the final cluster configuration and solution quality.

sections.title: Expectation-Maximization Algorithm
rules: The Expectation-Maximization algorithm finds maximum likelihood estimates in models with hidden variables.
In mixture models, cluster assignments are latent unobserved variables.
In the expectation step, the algorithm calculates the posterior probability that each component generated each point.
These posterior probabilities represent soft cluster responsibilities.
In the maximization step, the algorithm updates component priors, means, and covariances using the responsibilities.
Unlike k-means hard assignments, Expectation-Maximization performs soft probabilistic clustering.
Every iteration of Expectation-Maximization increases or maintains the data log likelihood.

sections.title: Mixtures of Latent Variable Models
rules: In high dimensions, estimating full covariance matrices for each mixture component causes overfitting.
Mixtures of factor analyzers fit a local factor analysis model within each cluster.
Mixtures of principal component analyzers fit local linear subspaces within each cluster.
Each local model reduces dimensionality while capturing cluster-specific correlations.

sections.title: Supervised Learning after Clustering
rules: Unsupervised clustering can discover useful representations for subsequent supervised tasks.
We can replace raw input features with distances or responsibilities computed from cluster centers.
Radial basis function neural networks use cluster centers as hidden unit prototypes.
Semi-supervised learning clusters large pools of unlabeled data and labels cluster centers using few labeled instances.

sections.title: Hierarchical Clustering
rules: Hierarchical clustering produces a nested tree of clusters called a dendrogram.
Agglomerative clustering starts with each instance in its own cluster and iteratively merges the closest pair.
Divisive clustering starts with all instances in one cluster and iteratively splits clusters.
Single linkage measures cluster distance as the distance between the closest pair of instances.
Complete linkage measures cluster distance as the distance between the farthest pair of instances.
Average linkage measures cluster distance as the average distance between all instance pairs.
Ward's method merges clusters that produce the smallest increase in total within-cluster variance.

sections.title: Choosing the Number of Clusters
rules: Unsupervised learning lacks ground truth labels for evaluating validation performance directly.
An elbow plot shows cluster error against k to locate the point of diminishing returns.
Information criteria like AIC and BIC penalize mixture models for having too many parameters.
Cross-validation evaluates the likelihood of held-out validation data across different values of k.
External validation compares cluster results against known domain categories when available.

sections.title: Notes
rules: Arthur Dempster, Nan Laird, and Donald Rubin formalized the Expectation-Maximization algorithm in nineteen seventy-seven.
Stuart Lloyd developed the k-means algorithm at Bell Laboratories in nineteen fifty-seven.
Hierarchical clustering plays an essential role in biological taxonomy and phylogenetic trees.
